title: A constitutive law for magma that contains both crystals and bubbles

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a predictive relationship between deformation and stress in magma containing liquid silicate melt, solid crystals and gas bubbles. Such a constitutive law would describe how strongly the mixture resists flow, how that resistance changes with deformation rate, and how stress develops and relaxes when deformation changes over time. The target is a transferable description of the three-phase mixture across a broad, explicitly tested range of conditions.

Crystals and bubbles introduce different mechanical responses, and their combined effect may depend on how they interact. The supplied research describes bubbles as potentially increasing resistance in crystal-poor magma while facilitating deformation in crystal-rich magma. It identifies crystal concentration and capillary number—the relative importance of stresses deforming a bubble and surface tension restoring its shape—as important variables. These are the physical motivations reported in the research; the supplied review could not independently verify their experimental basis because retained source texts were unavailable.

The intended advance would explicitly represent interactions between crystals and bubbles. A common simplifying strategy described in the research treats one suspension as the effective surrounding fluid for the other. The concern is that this sequential construction can omit changes in local deformation, bubble shape and crystal organization caused by the phases acting together, particularly at high combined concentrations. Whether every existing approach fails over the intended domain cannot be established from the supplied evidence.

significance.text: A law that successfully predicts previously unmeasured three-phase behavior would provide a substantial new capability in magma rheology. Its direct output would be the relationship between stress and deformation across specified crystal and bubble concentrations, including whether apparent viscosity falls or rises as deformation rate increases. If independently validated for changing deformation, it would also predict transient stress and the dependence of apparent viscosity on deformation history. Revolutionary significance would depend on this predictive breadth; fitting a restricted collection of viscosity measurements would establish a narrower achievement.

The supplied research describes two-phase rheological laws as ingredients in magma-ascent models. A validated three-phase law could supply a more defensible stress calculation as crystals and bubbles evolve during ascent. This could improve investigations of pressure loss, flow localization and the conditions approaching fragmentation. These are conditional consequences of a successful constitutive model, and the supplied review could not verify the cited literature's account of existing model use.

Predicting whether a particular eruption will be explosive or effusive would require additional physical descriptions and validation, including gas permeability and escape, crystallization kinetics and brittle fragmentation. A successful rheological law would therefore be one component of an eruption model. Its possible wider value to multiphase-flow science would likewise depend on whether its treatment of interacting rigid and deformable inclusions transfers beyond the tested magmas.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability sought here is one constitutive framework that predicts both steady flow and time-dependent stress in crystal- and bubble-bearing magma across a broad, declared domain. The research presents limited experimental coverage and effective-medium nesting as obstacles. The stronger statement that no existing equation meets the entire target across basaltic and rhyolitic compositions remains unverified: the supplied review had no retained literature passages with which to establish that absence.

A central modeling challenge is determining which interaction variables are needed beyond the separate two-phase responses. Crystal concentration alone may not capture crystal shape, packing and contact structure; bubble concentration alone may not capture deformation and its effect on the surrounding flow. The framework must explain when the combined mixture changes between shear thinning and shear thickening and whether additional evolving structural variables are required to describe its deformation history. This is a synthesis of the proposed scientific problem, rather than a verified inventory of deficiencies in every published model.

Experimental validation must separate phase-interaction effects from differences in melt composition, crystal geometry and deformation history. The research reports that available experiments sample limited combinations of crystal and bubble fraction and often use analogue fluids. Tests spanning capillary numbers below and above one would examine different balances between bubble deformation and surface tension, but that coverage alone would not establish transfer between basaltic and rhyolitic melts. The extent of the reported experimental gaps remains uncertain without the source texts.

A particularly demanding hypothesis is that all necessary parameters can be fixed using only two-phase melts and then carried unchanged into three-phase predictions. Interactions present only when both suspended phases coexist may require information unavailable from either two-phase system separately. Whether that information can be derived from mechanics, or instead requires a limited three-phase calibration, is an open question in the proposed demonstration.

current_state.text: The supplied research identifies a British Society of Rheology review by Charalambides and coauthors, dated 30 September 2026, as describing a broadly applicable three-phase magma model as a major open challenge and calling for models that capture interactions beyond simple effective-medium constructions. This attribution comes from reported indexed text. The source index contains no retained copy, and the supplied review could not verify the passage or its context. It supports describing an attributed research agenda, while leaving the exact assessment of the field unresolved.

The research identifies Mader, Llewellin and Mueller's The rheology of two-phase magmas: A review and analysis, published on 1 May 2013 in Journal of Volcanology and Geothermal Research, volume 257, pages 135–158. It reports established descriptions for bubble-bearing melts that depend on capillary number and for crystal-bearing suspensions fitted to analogue and basaltic data, with poorer agreement for high-viscosity haplogranitic melts. It also describes limited three-phase analogue modeling at low bubble fraction. These descriptions were not independently verified in the supplied review; the ScienceDirect article record was identified, but no retained source text was available to check model scope or comparative performance.

For Pistone and coauthors' 2012 Deformation experiments of bubble- and crystal-bearing magmas, the research reports an indexed abstract describing hydrous haplogranite experiments with shear thinning at 55–65 volume percent crystals and shear thickening at 24 volume percent crystals, with 9–12 volume percent bubbles. Taken as reported, these are distinct experimental concentration regimes; they do not establish that an otherwise identical sample switches behavior solely because its crystal fraction changes. The numerical ranges are preserved as reported findings, but the supplied review could not inspect fraction definitions, experimental conditions or measurements in context.

The research additionally attributes an orders-of-magnitude viscosity reduction at high crystallinity to a bubble fraction near 0.1 in those experiments. That stronger quantitative claim remains unresolved because the supplied material lacks the measurements, comparison baseline and conditions needed to assess it. The absence of retained evidence does not show that the result is false. Even if confirmed, such a result would demonstrate an interaction under particular experimental conditions, rather than establish the proposed general constitutive law.

The supplied material does not establish that the proposed innovation has been achieved. It also contains no documented freshness-search coverage through 1 November 2026, so the completeness of this account of the current literature remains unresolved. The dated references and reported indexed findings provide research leads and context, with access limitations that prevent stronger conclusions about present-day model coverage.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed core demonstration: publish and fix the constitutive framework, parameter values, calibration data and prediction procedure before independent three-phase testing. The strongest version would calibrate parameters only on two-phase melts and predict three-phase responses without subsequent adjustment. If additional interaction parameters prove necessary, their calibration should be disclosed and separated from an independent validation set. Predeclare quantitative prediction tolerances so that success can be judged without adapting the criterion to the results.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed core demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed coverage would include crystal fractions from dilute conditions to about 0.6, bubble fractions from zero to several tenths, and capillary numbers below and above one. Define whether phase fractions refer to the total mixture or another reference volume, and test only physically admissible combinations. Include at least one natural or haplogranitic melt alongside any analogue fluids. These numerical ranges are proposed targets, not established community standards; results should state exactly which compositions, crystal geometries, bubble populations and deformation conditions were demonstrated.

completion_criteria.text: Measure complete steady flow curves to test apparent viscosity and the predicted shear-thinning or shear-thickening behavior. Add independent transient stress measurements, such as responses to starting, stopping or changing deformation rate, because steady viscosity agreement cannot validate the time-dependent part of the law. Reproduction using independently prepared samples and, preferably, another laboratory would test whether the predictive behavior survives changes in preparation and apparatus. A finite campaign would establish demonstrated breadth within its tested domain, not literal universality.

completion_criteria.text: As a separate application test, insert the fixed law into an existing one-dimensional ascent model and predict a change in fragmentation threshold before a decompression experiment. Specify the other physical closures, boundary conditions and their uncertainties, particularly those governing gas transport, crystallization and fragmentation. Agreement in the direction of change would provide preliminary evidence; a stronger result would predict its magnitude within predeclared uncertainty and distinguish the rheological contribution from the other closures.

related_concepts.text: RHE-01, A constitutive closure that still works in a flow it was not fitted to, shares the requirement of independent predictive transfer. RHE-10 makes that challenge specific to magma containing crystals and bubbles, including transfer from two-phase calibration to three-phase behavior. Success for this material system would address one concrete instance of the broader closure problem without establishing transfer for all complex fluids.

RHE-03, A continuum law for dense particulate flow from creep to inertia in an arbitrary shape, overlaps through concentrated crystals, packing and collective particle motion. RHE-10 additionally requires deformable gas bubbles and a melt matrix. RHE-02, A theory of amorphous yielding that predicts the yield stress and whether failure is brittle or ductile, overlaps where concentrated magma yields or approaches failure, but its central target differs from predicting the three-phase flow response. A magma constitutive law would not automatically provide a fragmentation or brittle-failure theory.

RHE-07, The local three-dimensional stress in a flowing material, without assuming the constitutive law, could offer a complementary route to independent stress validation if applicable under the relevant conditions. RHE-09, Computing viscoelastic flow at the elasticity of real processing, concerns reliable flow computation; RHE-10 concerns the material relationship that a calculation would use. Accurate numerics and a predictive constitutive law remain distinct requirements.

RHE-04, Inverse molecular design of nonlinear polymer-melt rheology, and RHE-11, A topology-based rheology of ring polymers, from pure melts to threaded states, share the broader ambition of connecting material structure to nonlinear flow. Their molecular and topological mechanisms differ from interactions among crystals, bubbles and silicate melt. RHE-05, A constitutive theory of active stress that can be inverted for a mechanical task, adds internally generated active stress and inverse design, neither of which defines the magma target.

RHE-06, Addressable solid–fluid switching that stays put without a sustaining field or settling particles, concerns controllable and persistent material states; RHE-10 seeks to predict magma response as its conditions and phase populations change. RHE-08, A predictive theory of elasto-inertial turbulence and of the drag-reduction ceiling, concerns turbulent-flow mechanisms and limits rather than this three-phase constitutive relationship. These distinctions follow from the supplied roster titles. The separate historical calibration list mentioned in the research was not supplied, so the claimed absence of a historical counterpart cannot be assessed.

change_log.change: Preserved RHE-10 and its title while defining the proposed law in terms of steady and transient stress response.
change_log.reason: The innovation's identity is coherent despite unresolved support for some literature assertions.

change_log.change: Qualified the categorical claim that no existing law spans the intended domain.
change_log.reason: The supplied review lacked retained source texts and freshness-search coverage needed to establish a universal absence claim.

change_log.change: Integrated phase-interaction mechanisms and the limits of effective-medium nesting without presenting those limitations as independently verified across all models.
change_log.reason: These details explain the scientific target, while their literature support remains constrained by source access.

change_log.change: Preserved the reported publication dates and experimental concentration ranges with explicit attribution and access limitations.
change_log.reason: Useful quantitative detail should remain available without implying inspection or validation beyond the supplied review.

change_log.change: Separated the reported shear-thinning and shear-thickening concentration regimes and qualified the orders-of-magnitude viscosity-reduction claim.
change_log.reason: Different experimental regimes do not establish a controlled single-variable transition, and the stronger viscosity claim lacks the contextual measurements needed for assessment.

change_log.change: Added independent transient testing, declared tolerances, fraction conventions and physically admissible combinations to the completion proposal.
change_log.reason: Steady flow curves alone cannot validate an unsteady constitutive law, and quantitative coverage requires unambiguous definitions.

change_log.change: Retained two-phase-only calibration as the strongest proposed test while identifying its feasibility as an open hypothesis.
change_log.reason: Three-phase interaction parameters may not be identifiable from two-phase data alone.

change_log.change: Separated constitutive validation from the proposed fragmentation application test and limited the interpretation of directional agreement.
change_log.reason: Fragmentation predictions depend on additional physical closures and uncertainties.

change_log.change: Explained overlap and distinctions across the supplied roster and removed the unverified assertion of no historical counterpart.
change_log.reason: The roster supports conceptual comparisons, but the separate historical list was unavailable.

unresolved_issues: The three source records contain no retained texts, preventing independent verification of reported passages, model limitations and experimental findings.
The exact conditions, phase-fraction definitions and comparison baseline for the reported orders-of-magnitude viscosity reduction near bubble fraction 0.1 remain unresolved.
No documented freshness-search coverage establishes whether work available through 1 November 2026 already meets some or all of the proposed capability.
It remains unknown whether two-phase calibration alone can determine the interaction terms needed for predictive three-phase rheology.
The required structural variables and demonstrated transfer across melt compositions, crystal geometries and deformation histories remain open.
Quantitative tolerances, transient protocols, reproducibility requirements and practical domain boundaries still need to be specified for an actual demonstration.
The proposed fragmentation experiment requires explicit choices for additional physical closures and a method for separating their effects from the constitutive law.
The separate historical calibration list was not supplied, so the claimed absence of a historical counterpart remains unassessed.
